title: Meeting Teresa (1567)
hookLine: he joins her reform of the Carmelites: barefoot, poor, prayerful

lines: ABOUT TO LEAVE FOR MORE SILENCE.
cards: Medina del Campo, 1567. John is twenty-five, newly ordained, and restless. He's a Carmelite, but he wants more silence and more prayer than his house gives him.
He's quietly decided to leave and join the Carthusians, monks known for silence and solitude. Then someone tells a visiting nun about him. She's older, well known, and in town to open a new convent.
She asks to meet him. They talk. And by the end of the conversation, he isn't going anywhere.

teach.b: First, the word. Discalced comes from the Latin for unshod, without shoes. Teresa's reformed Carmelites were called the Discalced, the barefoot ones.
In practice they usually wore simple rope sandals, not bare feet on Spanish stone, but the name said what they were about: poverty, simplicity, a life stripped down for prayer. Second, the pitch.
Teresa told John he didn't need to leave the Carmelites to find silence. He could help her bring it back to them.

She was already reforming convents of nuns; now she wanted a house of friars living the same way: poor, enclosed, praying for hours a day. He agreed, on one condition: that she not make him wait too long.

In 1568 he moved into the first house of Discalced friars, a half-ruined farmhouse in a tiny hamlet called Duruelo. The choir for prayer was up in the loft, so low at the sides that the friars had to stoop.
Teresa visited and said later it moved her deeply. That's when he took a new name, John of the Cross. Fourth, the shoes.
At the burning bush, God tells Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."

teach.h: PUT OFF THE SHOES FROM THY FEET.
teach.b: Taking off shoes is an old sign: you're somewhere holy, and you're not in charge here. The Discalced wanted to live their whole life that way. Not everyone welcomed the reform, though.
Tomorrow, how some of John's own brothers answered it.

how: The Discalced Carmelites, friars and nuns, still live Teresa and John's reform today, with hours of daily silent prayer, and many wear sandals as part of their habit.

o: set apart: friars who left their order to live alone
well shod: friars given sturdy boots for the road
without shoes: Teresa's barefoot reformed Carmelites

games.q: you're a young priest who wants a life of silent prayer. you're about to leave for monks known for silence, and a well-known nun asks you to stay and help her reform your own order. what do you do?
o: leave for the Carthusians as planned.
stay, and help her, as long as she doesn't make you wait.
stay, but keep out of the reform.
games.why: he agreed, on the condition that she not make him wait long. within a year he was living in a half-ruined farmhouse at Duruelo.

practice: If you can, slip off your shoes and feel the floor under your feet; if you're driving or can't, just picture it. Let your feet rest flat and notice the ground holding you up.
If you pray, treat this little spot as holy ground and simply be present to God there; if you don't, let the bare feet remind you to slow down and be where you are.

wordCard.voice: Discalced. From the Latin for unshod: Teresa and John's reformed Carmelites, living poor, simple and prayerful, often in rope sandals. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: unshod, from dis- (without) and calceus (shoe). the root of Discalced.

carryVoice: Your line: the barefoot friars. Poor, simple, and standing on holy ground. Day two hundred fifty-six, done.
